spec.topic: Should schools replace traditional report cards with twice-yearly parent-teacher conferences?

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: Schools should replace traditional report cards with twice-yearly parent-teacher conferences. Families need a fuller conversation about how children are doing.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: The district prints its report cards on pale blue paper. That detail is hardly central, but it is oddly familiar to parents.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: Traditional report cards give families little explanation for the grades a child receives; that limitation is one reason to replace them. Because parents need more detail, they can ask follow-up questions during parent-teacher conferences.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: A twice-yearly conference schedule gives every family two guaranteed conversations with teachers, which is another reason to make conferences the standard form of reporting.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: However, parent-teacher conferences take teachers away from lesson planning and marking, so replacing report cards would create a serious workload problem.

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: Because parents can ask follow-up questions, in other words, Annelise's proposal is that schools should replace traditional report cards with twice-yearly parent-teacher conferences.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: Parent-teacher conferences reveal the circumstances behind a child's academic performance. That fuller understanding is a further reason to adopt the replacement.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: My classroom has three windows, and the afternoon sun makes the projector difficult to see.

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: To put Annelise's proposal another way, it means making scheduled conversations the main form of reporting to parents.

spec.topic: Should households keep a shared emergency cash fund for unexpected expenses?

utterances.speaker: Samir
utterances.text: Good evening, we are live from the old mill studio. Tonight's question: should households keep a shared emergency cash fund for unexpected expenses? Quentin, you start.

utterances.speaker: Quentin
utterances.text: Every household should keep a shared emergency cash fund, because unexpected bills like a boiler failure arrive without warning.

utterances.speaker: Samir
utterances.text: Jelena, do you agree?

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: Yes. Borrowing to cover a sudden bill costs far more than paying from savings, which is another reason. Mine lives in a biscuit tin, I admit.

utterances.speaker: Clement
utterances.text: But a fund like that just sits idle, since inflation steadily erodes the value of cash.

utterances.speaker: Quentin
utterances.text: In other words, Clement, you think the money is wasted.

utterances.speaker: Valentina
utterances.text: Every household should have one because a fund is insurance rather than an investment. Nobody judges a smoke alarm by its returns, after all.

utterances.speaker: Samir
utterances.text: So you are saying, Valentina, that the fund should be judged by the protection it gives. We will take a vote after the break.

spec.topic: Should annual bonuses depend more on team performance than individual targets?

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: Welcome to the debate. Should annual bonuses depend more on team performance than on individual targets? Laleh, you support a stronger team component.

utterances.speaker: Laleh
utterances.text: Team-based bonuses encourage employees to help one another because shared targets make cooperation materially relevant.

utterances.speaker: Femi
utterances.text: Individual targets make personal contributions easier to evaluate. Some employees work on projects whose outcomes depend on several departments.

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: Femi raises the issue of fairness in measuring individual effort. Laleh, how would your approach preserve accountability?

utterances.speaker: Laleh
utterances.text: In other words, team bonuses place greater value on cooperation than on isolated output.

utterances.speaker: Femi
utterances.text: But team bonuses can hide free riding, because one employee may benefit from colleagues' work without contributing equally.

utterances.speaker: Laleh
utterances.text: That risk is precisely why a mixed bonus formula can preserve individual accountability. Because of that safeguard, the bonus formula should include both team and individual measures.

utterances.speaker: Femi
utterances.text: So you are saying that a mixed bonus formula protects accountability while rewarding cooperation. That approach can also encourage employees to compete narrowly if individual targets dominate.

utterances.speaker: Laleh
utterances.text: Yes, and giving individual targets too much weight can damage cooperation.

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: Put another way, giving individual targets too much weight can undermine teamwork.

utterances.speaker: Laleh
utterances.text: That is why team performance should receive more weight than individual targets in annual bonuses.

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: Femi, your final response?

utterances.speaker: Femi
utterances.text: Large teams make it harder to see who is contributing. Since that problem affects evaluation, it is reasonable to give team results a larger role, provided individual evidence is not ignored.

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: The central proposal is therefore a stronger team component with some individual measurement retained. We will take the audience vote after the break.

spec.topic: Should publicly funded research be required to publish all results, including failed experiments?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Publicly funded research should be required to publish all results, including failed experiments, because taxpayers have paid for every experiment, whether it succeeded or not.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Unpublished failures waste public money through duplicated work, since researchers often repeat experiments that others have already run and abandoned.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Critics say mandatory publication would burden researchers with writing up work that has no obvious audience.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That ignores how little is asked: a short structured entry in an open registry takes only about an hour to complete.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I spent three years in a university chemistry laboratory, so none of this is abstract to me.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Journals prefer positive findings, which means the published literature gives a skewed picture of what works.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, publishing all results would correct that skew. A full record of negative results would also let reviewers judge how strong a positive finding really is.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Funders could enforce the rule by withholding the final grant payment until the registry entry is filed. Put differently, researchers would have a direct financial reason to comply.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Some results, such as those involving patient data, cannot be published in full.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: But the requirement can allow anonymised summaries in place of raw data.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Open registries already exist in clinical trials.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Science works better when failure is treated as information rather than embarrassment.

spec.topic: Should criminal trials require unanimous jury verdicts in every serious offence?

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Should every serious criminal offence require a unanimous jury verdict?

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: A unanimous verdict gives every juror equal power to prevent a conviction. For that reason, serious criminal trials should require unanimous verdicts.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What is the practical effect of giving each juror that power?

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Because serious-trial unanimity gives every juror that veto, one juror's reasonable doubt can block a conviction.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Critics say that rule gives too much influence to a single juror.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: I served on a mock jury during university.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Could unanimity make trials unnecessarily slow?

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Unanimous deliberation can delay a trial when jurors disagree.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Then why not allow a qualified majority?

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Public confidence in verdicts matters more than the small efficiency gains from majority verdicts. For that reason, the law should accept the modest delay caused by unanimous deliberation. However, that delay is an acceptable cost, not a reason to abandon unanimity.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Are there safeguards against a juror who refuses to deliberate properly?

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Judges can dismiss jurors for misconduct. Because that safeguard removes improper holdouts, it protects unanimous verdicts without abandoning the unanimity rule.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In other words, judicial removal of a misconduct juror protects unanimous verdicts.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: To state my position plainly, every serious offence should be tried under a unanimous-verdict rule.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you mean that one reasonable doubt can prevent a conviction in a serious criminal trial?

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Yes, that is an important protection. Jury rooms should have better soundproofing.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What is your final reason for treating the verdict rule so seriously?

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Appeal courts cannot reliably reconstruct what happened during private jury deliberations. Because of that limitation, verdict rules deserve especially careful safeguards.

utterances.speaker: Yara

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What is the strongest reason for making unanimity mandatory?

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Unanimity protects defendants from conviction when the evidence leaves a reasonable doubt, because a single dissenting juror can identify a reasonable doubt that the majority has overlooked.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Critics say that gives one juror too much power.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: That criticism is fair: one unreasonable juror can prevent a justified conviction under a unanimity rule. I have discussed jury reform with several court reporters.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: How would you reduce that risk without abandoning unanimity?

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: A dissenting juror should be required to explain the objection to a conviction, because an unexplained veto should not be enough to stop a serious case.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are saying that one juror's objection can obstruct a verdict even when the objection is unreasonable?

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Yes. My position is that unanimity gives every juror an effective veto over a serious conviction.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In other words, you mean that a lone juror's ability to expose doubt is central to the case for unanimity.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Exactly. Serious cases also often involve circumstantial evidence, which often permits more than one plausible interpretation. That is why unanimity is particularly valuable when a serious case depends on circumstantial evidence.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Would this change the judge's role?

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: No. The judge would continue to explain the law to the jury under a unanimous-verdict rule.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Would the rule favour either side?

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: No. The unanimity requirement would apply equally to the prosecution and the defence.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Why does that equality matter?

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Applying the same unanimity requirement to both sides would make the rule procedurally even-handed. Procedural even-handedness is a reason to adopt the unanimity requirement.

spec.topic: Should manufacturers be required to sell replacement parts and repair manuals for electronic devices?

utterances.speaker: Enzo
utterances.text: Manufacturers should be required to sell replacement parts and repair manuals, since most devices get binned over one failed component like a battery or a screen.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: But that ignores safety: unvetted third-party parts create a fire risk, because badly fitted lithium batteries have already caused house fires.

utterances.speaker: Valentina
utterances.text: So you are saying, Xavier, that untrained repairs are a fire hazard.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: I bought a tablet last year and it already has a cracked screen.

utterances.speaker: Valentina
utterances.text: Requiring parts to be sold would also cut electronic waste, because devices could stay in use for years longer.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: So you are saying fewer devices would end up in landfill.

utterances.speaker: Enzo
utterances.text: Independent shops would also undercut manufacturers, since they already charge about a third of the manufacturer price wherever they can get parts.

utterances.speaker: Valentina
utterances.text: Unrelated, but the thread about the old forum rules got locked yesterday.

utterances.speaker: Enzo
utterances.text: Put another way, owners would pay far less at an independent shop than at the manufacturer.

spec.topic: Should managers be required to advertise internal candidates before recruiting externally?

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: Managers should be required to advertise internal candidates before recruiting externally. Internal candidates already understand our systems and culture, which is why I support the requirement.

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: I support it for another reason: advertising an internal opportunity gives qualified employees a fair chance to apply.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: External recruitment can identify applicants with skills that current employees do not have. That is a serious objection to making internal advertising mandatory.

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: Employees may feel overlooked when managers recruit externally without considering them, and that is a reason to require an internal advertisement.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: However, mandatory internal advertising can add several days to recruitment. Urgent hiring can lose strong applicants when the process takes an extra week, which is why the delay matters.

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: I have a separate concern: an emergency vacancy sometimes has to be filled within a week.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: To put it another way, the proposed rule is to advertise internally before recruiting outside the organization.

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: In other words, the proposed policy gives qualified internal employees a fair chance to apply.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: For context, I have personally managed six recruitment campaigns.

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: A transparent internal process improves employees' trust in promotion decisions, which is another reason to adopt the requirement.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: Because a public internal posting lets every eligible employee see that the same opportunity was available, it makes the process more credible.

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: So the rule would require an internal advertisement before an external search, not ban external recruitment.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: Put simply, managers would have to look inside the organization first and go outside only afterward.

spec.topic: Should planning rules require every new home to include a rainwater-collection system?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Planning rules should require every new home to include a rainwater-collection system, because water demand in the region is rising faster than supply.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A tank can cover toilet flushing and garden watering, which is a further reason, since together those make up around a third of what a household uses.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Timing matters too: installing a tank during construction costs far less than fitting one to a finished house, and that is why the rule should apply to new builds.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Critics reply that a tank in every new home would add a cost to houses that buyers are already struggling to afford.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: But that ignores how small the added cost is, roughly the price of a kitchen worktop, and it is recovered through lower water bills.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I grew up in a house with a large barrel under the downpipe, and I never thought of it as a burden.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Mandatory tanks would also ease pressure on storm drains during heavy downpours.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, every new home would hold back some of its own runoff.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Some councils have already adopted such rules without any sign of a slowdown in building.

spec.topic: Should mobile operating systems be required to allow alternative app stores?

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight: should mobile operating systems be forced to allow alternative app stores? Ulla, you start.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: Yes, they should, because the dominant app stores take up to thirty percent commission on every sale.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Florin, you work with developers.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: I agree with Ulla, since developers have no realistic alternative way to reach customers. Also, competition between stores would push commissions down.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Rashid, you disagree.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: I do, because alternative stores would expose users to malware.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Why are you so sure?

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: The platform owners' review process is what keeps phones safe, which is why that exposure matters. My niece lost her savings to a fake banking app last year.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Ulla?

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: Users could be forced onto risky stores to get the apps they want, since that is how it works for games. So, in other words, alternative stores would be dangerous for ordinary users.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Florin, is that fair?

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Not entirely. Safety would remain in users' hands, as installing from outside the official store would need a deliberate warning-screen opt-in.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Rashid, a quick reply.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: That is no safeguard at all, because most people tap through warning screens without reading them.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Europe has been through this.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Europe has already introduced rules of this kind.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Time is nearly up, so a last word. Ulla.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: Adopt the rule, with strong security standards.

spec.topic: Should pharmacies be allowed to prescribe routine antibiotics for minor infections without a doctor’s appointment?

utterances.speaker: Imogen
utterances.text: Our question is whether pharmacies should prescribe routine antibiotics for minor infections without a doctor's appointment. Thandiwe, why do you support the change?

utterances.speaker: Thandiwe
utterances.text: Pharmacies should be allowed to prescribe routine antibiotics for minor infections without a doctor's appointment. The reason is that this would make treatment more accessible for people who cannot quickly see a doctor.

utterances.speaker: Hamza
utterances.text: I support the proposal because trained pharmacists can identify uncomplicated infections by using clear clinical protocols.

utterances.speaker: Enzo
utterances.text: But minor infection symptoms can conceal serious illnesses that require a doctor's examination. That risk makes prescribing at the pharmacy unsafe.

utterances.speaker: Thandiwe
utterances.text: A further reason for allowing the policy is that pharmacy prescribing would reduce pressure on already crowded general-practice appointments.

utterances.speaker: Hamza
utterances.text: Another reason is that a pharmacist can refer a patient to a doctor when the symptoms do not fit a routine infection.

utterances.speaker: Imogen
utterances.text: Enzo, does the proposal include safeguards, or would every customer simply receive antibiotics?

utterances.speaker: Hamza
utterances.text: The policy would apply only to uncomplicated cases assessed under an approved protocol.

utterances.speaker: Thandiwe
utterances.text: So you are saying the policy would be restricted to straightforward infections assessed under official clinical rules.

utterances.speaker: Enzo
utterances.text: Every pharmacy taking part would need trained staff and a system for referring uncertain cases to doctors.

utterances.speaker: Hamza
utterances.text: In other words, participating pharmacies would require trained staff and a formal route for sending doubtful cases to doctors.

utterances.speaker: Thandiwe
utterances.text: The pharmacy near my home opens at seven o'clock in the morning.

utterances.speaker: Hamza
utterances.text: I have never liked the smell of antiseptic in medical waiting rooms.

utterances.speaker: Enzo
utterances.text: The Northmere pilot recorded fewer general-practice visits for minor infections; that result makes extending pharmacy access worthy of a national trial.

utterances.speaker: Imogen
utterances.text: Thank you. We have heard arguments about access, safeguards, and the danger of missing serious illness.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer

utterances.speaker: Agnieszka
utterances.text: That reliable record would preserve the exact context of an interrogation. The exact exchanges would remain available for later review.

utterances.speaker: Malik

utterances.speaker: Agnieszka
utterances.text: Because coercive tactics can be exposed, livestreaming gives supervisors a practical audit trail. In other words, livestreaming makes coercive interrogation practices easier for supervisors to audit.

utterances.speaker: Alina

utterances.speaker: Dolores

utterances.speaker: Dolores

utterances.speaker: Imogen

utterances.speaker: Imogen
utterances.text: Dolores, put another way, you are arguing that youth football leagues should not adopt a blanket heading prohibition without stronger evidence.

utterances.speaker: Florin

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: Yes, every secondary school should require a financial-literacy course before graduation, because so many young adults take on debt without understanding how interest works.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: Young people who don't pick up money skills at school often never pick them up at all, since families differ so widely in what they teach. That is also why I think a requirement is justified.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: In other words, for many students school is the only place they will ever be taught about money.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: But the usual objection is that the timetable is already too crowded to add a required course.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: A single semester is enough to cover budgeting, credit and saving, so the cost to the timetable is small, and that is why I would still go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: I should say I taught maths for eleven years before joining a consumer-advice charity.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: The regional pilot shows it works, since its students borrowed less in their first year after school. Put another way, the course pays off in lower borrowing.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: That matters because graduates start earning and borrowing within a year of leaving school, which is why debt knowledge cannot wait.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: My nephew has just opened his first bank account, as it happens.

utterances.text: Item two: whether voting should be compulsory. Kai, would you open?

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: I think voting should be compulsory with a modest penalty for unjustified abstention, because compulsory systems raise turnout far above voluntary ones.

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: And higher turnout matters, since it makes results more representative of the whole population, which is why I lean towards Kai's view.

utterances.speaker: Babajide

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: Noted. Babajide, is there more you want to say on that?

utterances.speaker: Babajide
utterances.text: Yes, we would get lots of random ballots. What I mean is that many compelled voters would not know the candidates or the issues.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: Aside: my office lease runs out in March, so I may be late next month.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: On freedom, though, a fine of twenty pounds is small enough that it is not coercion, since people in Australia have long accepted a small fine.

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: Fair. What about the effect on the parties?

utterances.speaker: Babajide

utterances.text: Facial recognition can identify suspected fare evaders within seconds. Because that speed lets inspectors check more vehicles quickly, authorities could reduce prolonged ticket inspections.

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: But that recommendation is unsafe: facial recognition can wrongly flag passengers who have paid their fares. Independent audits found a significant error rate in the proposed system, which is why the risk cannot be dismissed.

utterances.speaker: Aurelio
utterances.text: Priya's position is that public transport authorities should deploy facial recognition against fare evasion; in other words, Priya recommends using the system. utterances.text: Should businesses replace fixed holiday allowances with unlimited paid leave?

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: Yes. Businesses should replace fixed holiday allowances with unlimited paid leave, because fixed allowances encourage employees to take days they do not need.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you think businesses should reconsider fixed holiday allowances because those allowances encourage unnecessary leave?

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: That recommendation is too broad. On the contrary, the proposal is unlimited paid leave rather than compulsory leave-taking; in other words, employees would still choose when to be away.

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: For context, I have worked in human resources for eight years.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What would stop unlimited leave from making staffing unpredictable?

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: Shared team calendars make planned absences visible to managers, and because those absences are visible, managers can maintain adequate staffing under an unlimited-leave policy.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In other words, unlimited paid leave is the proposed replacement for fixed holiday allowances.

utterances.speaker: Jasper

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In other words, your central point is that voting at sixteen would provide practical civic experience. Critics might still say that the knowledge gap makes the proposal unacceptable.

spec.topic: Should schools abolish class rankings to reduce unhealthy competition among students?

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: Welcome to tonight's debate. Should schools abolish class rankings to reduce unhealthy competition among students?

utterances.speaker: Leilani
utterances.text: Some students hide mistakes to protect their position in the class ranking. That is why I believe class rankings intensify unhealthy competition.

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: Leilani, are you calling for the rankings to disappear altogether?

utterances.speaker: Leilani
utterances.text: Yes. Schools should abolish class rankings, because they turn learning into a contest for status.

utterances.speaker: Rohan
utterances.text: I disagree with abolishing them outright. Rankings can give students a clear benchmark, but I accept that regular portfolio reviews give students opportunities to reflect on their learning.

utterances.speaker: Rohan
utterances.text: For that reason, portfolio work and conferences can provide more useful feedback than a public ranking.

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: What would replace the ranking in practice?

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: Class rankings can motivate some students to work harder, though they can also make every result feel like a public judgment.

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: Leilani, what system would you put in its place?

utterances.speaker: Leilani
utterances.text: Schools should replace public rankings with portfolios and individual conferences, so students can discuss progress without competing over a single number.

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: So you are saying that portfolios and individual conferences should replace public rankings.

utterances.speaker: Rohan
utterances.text: In other words, class rankings can motivate some students to work harder, but that benefit does not require publishing an order of merit.

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: Teachers can assess students without publicly ordering them from highest to lowest; therefore, student assessment can continue without a public class ranking.

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: Rohan, what is the strongest objection to the proposal?

utterances.speaker: Rohan
utterances.text: Abolishing rankings would remove a useful incentive for some students. I still think that objection is outweighed by the harm caused by constant comparison.

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: I have taught at this school for eight years.

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: For context, the school library is open until six o'clock on weekdays.

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: Since rankings intensify unhealthy competition, and assessment can continue without a public ranking, abolishing class rankings is the best way for schools to reduce unhealthy competition while preserving meaningful assessment.

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: I think election day should become a public holiday. The reason is that a public holiday would give shift workers time to vote.

utterances.speaker: Marisol
utterances.text: Many hourly workers cannot leave work during polling hours. That is why a holiday would help people who are currently shut out.

utterances.speaker: Marisol
utterances.text: But employers would lose a day's output if election day became a public holiday.

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: Existing early voting does not reach everyone, because thirty-eight percent of low-income voters skipped it in the last election.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: The election commission offers only two weeks of early voting. Many shift workers cannot attend early voting during those two weeks, which is another reason the current system has limited reach.

utterances.speaker: Marisol
utterances.text: So you are saying, in other words, that hourly workers often cannot get away from work to vote.

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: As a side note, my neighborhood holds a farmers' market every Saturday.

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: Marisol's concern about lost output is credible because small employers often cannot replace absent workers.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: Some countries that hold elections on holidays report higher turnout. A 2024 comparative study found higher average turnout in countries with election holidays, which is why I support considering the change.

utterances.speaker: Marisol
utterances.text: Put another way, international evidence links election holidays with higher turnout.

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: A public holiday would make voting a more visible civic event, and that visibility is another reason to adopt it.

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: A holiday would turn voting into a prominent shared civic occasion; that is what I mean by making voting more visible.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: However, a public holiday would not by itself guarantee high turnout. Turnout also depends on registration access and voter information, because people cannot vote if they are not prepared or registered.

utterances.speaker: Marisol
utterances.text: So the proposal is to give people a common day on which voting is easier and more visible.

utterances.text: Our question is whether councils should let residents vote directly on how a fixed portion of the annual budget is spent. Chidi, you support the proposal.

utterances.text: Residents should directly choose spending priorities for a fixed portion of the annual budget.

utterances.speaker: Dolores
utterances.text: Participatory budgeting would allow residents to decide a defined portion of the annual budget, not the entire budget.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: To put my position plainly, direct resident voting should determine how a fixed share of the annual budget is spent. Because residents know their neighbourhood priorities, this would make council spending reflect local priorities more closely.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: The reason to limit the scheme is that direct resident voting would give residents meaningful control without handing them the entire budget.

utterances.speaker: Dolores
utterances.text: In other words, participatory budgeting would let residents decide a defined slice of the annual budget rather than the whole budget. Because the slice is defined in advance, direct voting would be manageable for residents and councils.

utterances.speaker: Dolores
utterances.text: That boundary also protects funding for essential services, which is why limiting the vote to a defined budget slice matters.

utterances.speaker: Gabriela

utterances.speaker: Gabriela

utterances.speaker: Gabriela

utterances.speaker: Chidi

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight's question: once children type fluently, should primary schools still teach handwriting? Siobhan, you first.

utterances.speaker: Siobhan
utterances.text: Yes. Schools should keep teaching handwriting even after pupils type fluently.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: What is your evidence?

utterances.speaker: Siobhan
utterances.text: Brain scans show that forming letters by hand fires up the brain's reading areas more than typing does. That is why children learn letters faster by hand, and it is also a reason to keep handwriting in the timetable.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tobias, you disagree.

utterances.speaker: Tobias
utterances.text: But the primary timetable is already crowded, and that is why handwriting should stop after the first two years.

utterances.speaker: Tobias
utterances.text: Handwriting is no longer a useful everyday skill, since almost all adult writing now happens on keyboards or phones.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So you are saying that nobody needs to write with a pen any more.

utterances.speaker: Bilal
utterances.text: Pupils still need legible handwriting, because many national exams are still handwritten at sixteen.

utterances.speaker: Siobhan
utterances.text: Handwriting practice also strengthens fine motor control in young children, because occupational therapists report that pupils who skip pencil work reach secondary school with weaker hand strength.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: In other words, pen work is physical training for small hands.

utterances.speaker: Bilal
utterances.text: Handwritten notes are remembered better than typed notes, since in one university trial students who took notes by hand scored higher on conceptual questions than those who typed.

utterances.speaker: Siobhan
utterances.text: Put another way, what you write by hand stays in your head better than what you type.

utterances.speaker: Tobias
utterances.text: I should say that I typed my first story at the age of six.

utterances.speaker: Bilal
utterances.text: The school inspectorate publishes its new writing guidance next spring.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, to sum up, Siobhan's case is that handwriting stays on the timetable even for fluent typists.

spec.topic: Should professional basketball teams be required to disclose players’ injury details before every game?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Professional basketball teams should be required to disclose players' relevant injury details before every game, because current pregame reports often use vague labels such as questionable without explaining a player's limitations.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Because those labels are vague, fans cannot tell whether a player is likely to participate. That uncertainty therefore distorts public expectations about the game.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Disclosing diagnoses when appropriate, expected minutes, and physical limitations would make injury reports useful. In other words, useful injury disclosure would explain what a player's participation actually means.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Some injury details are private medical information.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: However, a blanket disclosure rule could pressure players to compete while injured.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A narrower rule can protect diagnoses while requiring teams to report functional information. For that reason, the narrower rule justifies requiring teams to disclose relevant injury details before games.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The author still keeps a paper ticket from a college basketball game.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Transparent reports improve competitive fairness because opponents can prepare more accurately when they know which players are limited.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, a useful report describes a player's capacity rather than merely listing participation status.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The author's favorite basketball arena serves unusually poor coffee.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A disclosure deadline several hours before tipoff would give opponents time to prepare, and that preparation would make the disclosure rule fairer.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put plainly, professional basketball teams should be required to disclose relevant player injury details before every game.

utterances.speaker: Vikram
utterances.text: Compromised employee accounts are a common route into company systems, and keystroke and mouse monitoring can reveal unusual account use quickly.

utterances.speaker: Laleh
utterances.text: Employers should be allowed to monitor workers’ keystrokes and mouse movements when they give workers clear notice, because compromised employee accounts are a common route into company systems and because such monitoring can reveal unusual account use quickly.

utterances.speaker: Hiroshi
utterances.text: But routine monitoring of keystrokes and mouse movements can turn ordinary work into surveillance of employees’ personal habits. That objection matters even when workers receive notice.

utterances.speaker: Moderator

spec.topic: Should gene editing be permitted to prevent inherited diseases in human embryos?

utterances.speaker: Zofia
utterances.text: The agenda asks whether gene editing should be permitted to prevent inherited diseases in human embryos. I suggest we separate the medical benefits from the safety and justice concerns.

utterances.speaker: Zofia
utterances.text: Inherited diseases can cause severe lifelong suffering. Because of that, gene editing in human embryos can prevent some inherited diseases.

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: Gene editing in human embryos can introduce unintended genetic changes. Because those changes may be serious, current safety evidence is insufficient for clinical use.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: Current laboratory methods can detect some unintended genetic changes before implantation. For that reason, clinical use could be considered after rigorous testing.

utterances.speaker: Zofia
utterances.text: Changes made to human embryos could affect future descendants. Since future descendants cannot consent to those changes, this raises a special ethical concern.

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: A prohibition would deny families at risk a possible way to prevent inherited diseases. That is why a carefully limited permission could be ethically preferable to an absolute ban.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: Germline gene editing could widen inequality if access to it is expensive. Therefore, public funding would be needed to make access equitable.

utterances.speaker: Zofia
utterances.text: Before we decide, I want the oversight requirements recorded clearly.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: The university ethics committee will meet on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: Since laboratory methods can reveal unintended changes before implantation, rigorous oversight can reduce the risk of hidden harms.

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: To put Zofia's proposal another way, the proposal is to use embryo gene editing to prevent inherited diseases, not to select cosmetic traits.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: So you are saying that embryo gene editing is not yet safe enough for clinical use.

utterances.speaker: Zofia
utterances.text: Put another way, a limited permission would be preferable to a blanket prohibition.

utterances.speaker: Zofia
utterances.text: However, that conclusion is too strong: insufficient safety evidence does not by itself justify a permanent prohibition on embryo gene editing.

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: The draft agenda contains six items.

utterances.speaker: Zofia

utterances.speaker: Orla

utterances.speaker: Zofia
utterances.text: The same uncertainty is why clinical use should be delayed: the uncertainty surrounding embryo editing justifies delaying clinical use.

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: A carefully regulated programme could generate evidence about the safety of embryo editing. For that reason, a carefully regulated programme should be allowed to study embryo editing.

utterances.speaker: Orla

utterances.speaker: Efua

utterances.speaker: Zofia

utterances.speaker: Efua

spec.topic: Should councils require landlords to install basic energy-efficiency measures before renewing rental licences?

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight: should councils make landlords install basic energy-efficiency measures before renewing a rental licence? Priya, you start.

utterances.speaker: Priya
utterances.text: Yes, they should, because tenants in poorly insulated homes pay far more for heating than other households. And cold, damp homes also damage their health, which is another reason.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Alejandro, you disagree.

utterances.speaker: Alejandro
utterances.text: I do, because landlords will pass the cost of the installations on to tenants through higher rents. The requirement would make rents rise.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, Alejandro, in other words you are saying the rule would push rents up for tenants.

utterances.speaker: Priya
utterances.text: Insulation lowers heating bills by more than a typical rent increase would add.

utterances.speaker: Emeka

utterances.speaker: Emeka
utterances.text: A little: my own street has two rental houses with new boilers. But what I mean is that the rule would hit small landlords hardest and shrink the rental supply.

utterances.speaker: Priya
utterances.text: That is to say the problem is the upfront cost for small landlords, and the council could offer grants to cover it.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: We will take the audience's view after the break; the studio looks split.

spec.topic: Should retailers pay a levy on unnecessary plastic packaging around fresh produce?

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Should retailers pay a levy on unnecessary plastic packaging around fresh produce?

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Retailers should pay that levy because unnecessary plastic packaging creates disposal costs for councils and households.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What is the strongest reason for imposing it?

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: A second reason is that a levy would encourage retailers to reduce unnecessary plastic packaging.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Some retailers say the levy would punish businesses that already operate on narrow profit margins.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: But that concern targets the wrong policy: the levy would target avoidable packaging rather than every package used by retailers.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Would the levy cover protective wrapping as well as decorative wrapping?

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: It should apply only to plastic packaging that is unnecessary for protecting or transporting fresh produce.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you mean that the levy would not apply to every piece of plastic packaging.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Retailers could avoid the levy by switching to reusable crates and lighter packaging.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In other words, retailers could escape the levy by using reusable crates and less packaging.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Consumers should not bear the cost of unnecessary packaging through higher produce prices.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Elif is saying that shoppers should not pay for plastic packaging that retailers could avoid.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: A levy based on packaging weight would be the simplest system to administer, because retailers can record packaging weight more easily than they can classify every design feature.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: I buy fresh berries from a local shop every week. Retailers already record packaging weight for some supplier audits.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: The levy can be collected through existing packaging-data reports, because most large retailers already submit those reports to regulators.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In other words, existing packaging-data reports can be used to collect the levy, which is why retailers should pay it.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Would you support the proposal if the levy excluded genuinely necessary packaging?

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: I prefer buying loose apples when the shop has them.

utterances.speaker: Author

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: But the charge is unfair to low-income households who have to drive.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That objection ignores that the revenue can fund cheaper and more frequent bus services, since that gives those households an alternative.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, the charge would pay for better buses.

utterances.speaker: Author

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Shops in town centres could lose some customers who currently arrive by car.

utterances.speaker: Nadia

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru

utterances.speaker: Nadia

utterances.speaker: Vikram

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru

spec.topic: Should schools make swimming proficiency a requirement for joining competitive sports teams?

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Should schools make swimming proficiency a requirement for joining competitive sports teams?

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: Yes, schools should require swimming proficiency for students joining competitive sports teams, because swimming skills can help students respond safely to accidents near water.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Some parents worry that such a rule would be unfair to children who have never had swimming lessons. What is your response?

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: I have coached school athletics for eight years, but that experience is not the main issue.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: The concern is that a swimming requirement could exclude students who have had little access to pools.

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: Schools can provide free swimming lessons before applying the requirement. Because those lessons are available, schools can reduce the exclusion caused by the rule.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you propose making swimming proficiency a condition for joining any competitive school sports team.

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: Not quite. A swimming requirement should be limited to a short survival test rather than a racing standard.

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: A short survival test measures basic water safety rather than racing speed, which is why it is the appropriate standard.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In other words, you mean that the test should measure basic water safety, not swimming performance.

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: Exactly. Coaches can provide supervised swimming practice before team trials, and that makes the swimming requirement workable for students who initially lack confidence.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: The regional school sports finals are scheduled for May. Would schools have enough time to prepare students?

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: Yes. A standard swimming check is simple for schools to administer, so preparation need not delay team selection.

utterances.text: Should schools make swimming proficiency a requirement for joining competitive sports teams?

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: Yes, schools should require swimming proficiency before students join competitive sports teams. The reason is that competitive sports teams have a duty to protect students from avoidable physical danger.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Critics say that such a rule might be unfair to otherwise excellent athletes. What is your response?

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: That concern is real: a swimming requirement could exclude students who are talented at their chosen sport. In other words, schools should require swimming proficiency before students join competitive sports teams.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Why is swimming especially relevant to competitive teams?

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: Competitive sports teams regularly use pools and open-water venues for training, so students who cannot swim confidently could face danger during team activities.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Does that mean every student must already be a strong swimmer?

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: No. Because students who cannot swim confidently could face danger during team activities, a safety check before competitive-team enrollment is reasonable. However, a blanket swimming-proficiency rule could exclude capable athletes unnecessarily.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Could schools protect students without rejecting them immediately?

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: Yes. Schools can provide a short swimming assessment before team selection, because the assessment would identify students who need swimming lessons.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What should happen after the assessment?

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: Schools could direct weaker swimmers to lessons before allowing them to join a team. That support is why schools should require swimming proficiency before students join competitive sports teams.

utterances.text: For the record, when did you learn to swim, and what sports do you prefer?

spec.topic: Should national sports federations impose salary caps on professional leagues?

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should national federations impose salary caps on professional leagues? Rafael, you start.

utterances.speaker: Rafael
utterances.text: Yes, they should, because without caps the richest clubs simply buy the best players every year.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Ivana, your view?

utterances.speaker: Ivana
utterances.text: Competitions where a few clubs always win lose their unpredictability and their audiences, and that is why caps would keep them balanced.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Bernard, you disagree.

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: Caps would hold down player wages, and capped players would move to leagues abroad that pay more.

utterances.speaker: Ivana
utterances.text: That is a real risk, since my league has lost three internationals to overseas clubs in two years.

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: Exactly, so caps would drive the best players out of the country, but that objection stands against Rafael's proposal.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Rafael, is balance really the point?

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: Balance does not depend on caps at all, because revenue sharing spreads money more evenly between clubs.

utterances.speaker: Rafael
utterances.text: I should say I hold a season ticket at a mid-table club.

utterances.speaker: Rafael
utterances.text: The American football league has had a cap for decades, and different champions have won almost every recent season, which shows caps work.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Ivana, can you sum up that point?

utterances.speaker: Ivana
utterances.text: In other words, caps keep competitions balanced.

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: Caps are hard to enforce because clubs hide payments in side deals, and federations lack the power to audit them.

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: Put another way, caps are not workable in practice.

utterances.speaker: Rafael
utterances.text: So you are saying a cap only works if federations get real auditing powers, and I would give them those.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Before we close, a reminder that the cup final is on Saturday evening.

spec.topic: Should people be expected to return online purchases to physical shops?

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: Should people be expected to return online purchases to physical shops?

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: Yes, people should be expected to return online purchases to physical shops. I worked in a retail shop during university.

utterances.speaker: Malik
utterances.text: But that expectation is unfair, because many physical shops lack the space and staff to handle online returns.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: A shared shop-based return system would reduce packaging and delivery journeys, which is one reason to expect customers to use it.

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: Before we continue, I should mention that I prefer programmes about local history.

utterances.speaker: Nkechi
utterances.text: Online returns often require customers to print labels and arrange collection. Local shops would give customers a nearby place to return online purchases, and that is why the expectation is reasonable.

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: So you are saying that the proposal is to use local shops as nearby return points for online purchases?

utterances.speaker: Nkechi
utterances.text: Exactly. Because online returns often require customers to print labels and arrange collection, online returns are cumbersome for many customers. That is why people should be expected to use physical shops.

utterances.speaker: Selin
utterances.text: Most physical shops already have staffed customer-service counters, so those customer-service counters could handle modest return volumes.

utterances.speaker: Malik
utterances.text: A national return scheme would need clear standards for packaging and data security. Because of that, participating shops should follow the same packaging and data-security rules.

utterances.speaker: Selin

spec.topic: Should schools let students choose their own start times within a daily attendance window?

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: I think schools should let students choose their own start times within a daily attendance window. This could improve attendance because students could align school with their sleep needs and family routines.

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: I disagree. Schools need fixed start times to coordinate transportation reliably, because multiple bus departures would be difficult to coordinate if students arrived at different times.

utterances.speaker: Hamza
utterances.text: So you are saying that transportation problems make student-selected start times impractical?

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: In other words, my proposal is that students should be allowed to select their own start times within a defined attendance window.

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: The school cafeteria currently serves breakfast from 7:45 onward.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: The arrangement remains workable because a staggered schedule could give teachers predictable groups of students. That works because predictable student groups would let teachers plan lessons more effectively.

utterances.speaker: Hamza
utterances.text: A shared attendance app could assign students to start-time groups automatically; because of that, teachers could plan around those groups, which is why schools can offer the choice. I have two younger siblings who attend primary school.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether governments should ban the release of genetically modified mosquitoes. Aiko, you first.

utterances.speaker: Aiko
utterances.text: They should not ban it, because trial releases have cut local dengue-carrying mosquito populations by over ninety percent. That result is hard to ignore.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Dalia, you disagree.

utterances.speaker: Dalia
utterances.text: I do, and the reason is simple: a release cannot be recalled once the mosquitoes have spread into the wild. So governments should ban it.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Aiko, a reply?

utterances.speaker: Aiko
utterances.text: But the modified mosquitoes die out after a few generations, so the change does not persist.

utterances.speaker: Host

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Helga, go on.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: Bed nets and spraying have failed to stop dengue in many cities, which shows other methods are not enough on their own.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Pablo?

utterances.speaker: Pablo
utterances.text: Other mosquito species could fill the empty niche.

utterances.speaker: Dalia
utterances.text: In other words, removing one mosquito species could have knock-on effects on the ecosystem.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: Those effects are unproven and speculative, since the concerns are theoretical rather than demonstrated.

utterances.speaker: Pablo

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Pablo, any last point?

spec.topic: Should job applicants be told the salary before submitting an application?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Job applicants should be told the salary range before submitting an application. A salary range lets applicants decide whether a position fits their financial needs, which is why this information belongs at the start of the process.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Applicants who can assess financial fit early avoid wasting time on unsuitable applications. That matters especially because avoiding unsuitable applications particularly helps applicants who have limited time for a job search.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Some employers worry that publishing a salary range will deter applicants who expect higher pay. Even so, that concern does not outweigh the applicant's need for basic information.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A posted salary range is an early fit signal for applicants; in other words, it tells them whether the job is worth pursuing before they invest further effort.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Many applicants prepare for interviews outside their normal working hours.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Salary transparency can also reveal whether an employer has defined the responsibilities of a role.

spec.topic: Should patients with terminal illnesses have the legal right to request assisted dying?

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Yes, I believe terminally ill patients should have the legal right to request assisted dying, because competent adults have authority over their own bodies and the manner of their deaths.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Some patients have pain that palliative care simply cannot relieve, and that is why I say forcing them to endure it is cruel. Which is another reason the law should allow them to request help.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Opponents say elderly and vulnerable people could feel pressured into choosing death. But safeguards such as requiring two independent doctors make coercion much easier to detect.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Oregon has operated with such safeguards since 1997, which shows they work. Put another way, coercion is far easier to spot when two independent doctors must agree on a request.

utterances.speaker: Fatima

spec.topic: Should employers publish salary ranges in every job advertisement?

utterances.speaker: Leilani
utterances.text: Our question is whether employers should publish salary ranges in every job advertisement. Yusuf, make the case for it.

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: Many employers currently omit salary ranges from job advertisements. Publishing salary ranges would let applicants compare opportunities before applying.

utterances.speaker: Leilani
utterances.text: Arjun, what is the strongest objection?

utterances.speaker: Arjun
utterances.text: Arjun has worked in recruitment for eight years. I worry that a badly designed rule could create false confidence.

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: Publishing salary ranges would reduce applications from people who cannot accept the available pay, and it would make unjustified pay differences within a company easier to detect.

utterances.speaker: Leilani
utterances.text: Arjun, does a range solve the problem if the range is broad?

utterances.speaker: Arjun
utterances.text: Employers can use very wide salary ranges to conceal the pay they actually intend to offer, so very wide salary ranges can mislead applicants instead of helping them compare jobs.

utterances.speaker: Leilani
utterances.text: So you are saying that wide salary ranges can make advertised pay information misleading.

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: A legal minimum width for salary ranges is workable, and that requirement would make published salary ranges genuinely comparable.

utterances.speaker: Arjun
utterances.text: So you are proposing a rule that requires salary ranges to be wide enough to support meaningful comparison.

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: Yes, and publishing salary ranges would make unjustified differences in employees' pay more visible.

utterances.speaker: Arjun
utterances.text: Private salary negotiations can protect applicants who have unusual skills or circumstances.

utterances.speaker: Leilani
utterances.text: In other words, your concern is that private negotiation can protect applicants with unusual skills or circumstances.

utterances.speaker: Leilani
utterances.text: My conclusion is that employers should publish salary ranges in every job advertisement, because ranges let applicants compare opportunities, reduce unsuitable applications, expose unjustified pay differences, and become genuinely comparable when a minimum-width rule applies.

spec.topic: Should public schools provide free breakfast to every pupil, regardless of family income?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Public schools should provide free breakfast to every pupil, regardless of family income.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: This policy is necessary because some pupils arrive at school too hungry to concentrate well.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A second reason is that universal access to breakfast avoids marking some pupils as poor.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The primary schools in my district renovated their kitchens last year.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: School breakfast can help pupils begin the day ready to learn, which further supports this recommendation.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The case is stronger since providing breakfast at school can reduce the pressure on families during difficult mornings.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Another reason to adopt the policy is that a universal breakfast programme is simpler to administer than a programme that checks family income.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I usually ate breakfast at home during primary school.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: This recommendation is warranted because a free breakfast gives pupils a reliable opportunity to eat before lessons begin.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Finally, offering breakfast to all pupils can improve punctuality because children do not need to wait for food at home.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Critics raise one concern: universal breakfast provision would waste money on pupils from affluent families.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That objection is misplaced.

utterances.speaker: Author

spec.topic: Should criminal records for minor offences be automatically sealed after five crime-free years?

utterances.speaker: Birgit
utterances.text: Our question tonight is whether criminal records for minor offences should be automatically sealed after five crime-free years. Jelena, you support the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: I do: criminal records for minor offences should be automatically sealed after five crime-free years because five crime-free years usually indicate that a person poses a low risk of repeating a minor offence.

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: Automatic sealing would improve employment prospects for people with minor convictions, which is a second reason to adopt the rule.

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: So you are saying that minor criminal records should automatically disappear after five crime-free years. But automatic sealing could prevent employers from seeing a pattern of repeated offending.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: I still support the policy, because automatic sealing would let people return to work without carrying a minor conviction forever.

utterances.speaker: Birgit
utterances.text: Put another way, the proposal is a five-year clean-record rule for minor convictions.

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: One more reason for automatic sealing is that many minor convictions result from one-time mistakes rather than persistent offending.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: For offences outside the minor category, a review panel should handle sealing decisions. That is needed because a review panel can distinguish a serious pattern of offending from an isolated lapse.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: Judges already have access to fuller case files that would help a review panel make those decisions, which makes the safeguard workable.

utterances.speaker: Birgit
utterances.text: So your safeguard is human review for offences that are not minor.

utterances.speaker: Rosalind

spec.topic: Should clinical trials be required to include equal numbers of all major demographic groups?

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Our subject is whether clinical trials should be required to include equal numbers of all major demographic groups. Nkechi, please begin.

utterances.speaker: Nkechi
utterances.text: Clinical trials often produce less reliable evidence when major demographic groups are missing or underrepresented. That is my first reason for supporting the requirement.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: Equal representation would make it easier to detect differences in treatment effects and side effects across major demographic groups. That is another reason the requirement is justified.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: Because missing groups can weaken the evidence, and because equal representation can reveal group-specific effects, clinical trials should be required to include equal numbers of participants from all major demographic groups.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Gideon, what practical advantage would this rule have?

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: Community clinics can help sponsors recruit participants from groups that research hospitals often miss. That is a practical reason to require equal representation.

utterances.speaker: Nkechi
utterances.text: Participants are more likely to trust medical research when they see people like themselves included. That public-trust benefit is another reason to adopt the requirement.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: So you are saying that every clinical trial would have to include equal numbers from all major demographic groups.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Xavier, do you think the rule would improve the quality of the evidence?

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: A trial's conclusions are only as trustworthy as the sample on which those conclusions are based. That is why the proposed requirement is warranted.

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: In other words, the debate concerns mandatory equal representation of all major demographic groups in every clinical trial.

utterances.speaker: Nkechi
utterances.text: Equal recruitment would reduce the risk that a treatment appears safe only because an important group was not studied adequately. That is a further reason for requiring equal numbers.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: Sponsors could disclose recruitment gaps before regulators approve a trial's results. That transparency is another reason to support the proposed requirement.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: To put the proposal plainly, the rule would require clinical trials to enroll equal numbers from all major demographic groups.

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: What Nkechi is proposing is a requirement for equal demographic representation in every clinical trial.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: I disagree with that blanket requirement: equal numbers are not feasible for every disease, so the rule would be too rigid.

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: For context, I have worked on clinical-trial ethics committees for eight years.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Nkechi, does that objection change your position?

utterances.speaker: Nkechi
utterances.text: The studio's audience received information about the debate before the programme began. My position remains that the rule should be required, with narrowly defined exceptions.

utterances.speaker: Esther

utterances.speaker: Xavier

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: Gideon, what should regulators actually require?

utterances.speaker: Gideon

utterances.speaker: Xavier

utterances.speaker: Esther

utterances.speaker: Gideon

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: Put another way, the urgent-treatment exception means that an enrollment rule should not postpone access to a needed treatment.

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: I disagree: schools should keep homework deadlines during major religious holidays. The reason is that consistent deadlines prevent assignments from piling up afterward.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: So you are saying that schools should require homework deadlines during major religious holidays. Many families plan their religious observances across several days, and that is another reason to adopt a ban.

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: Some students do not observe every major religious holiday. Several students also work part-time on weekends.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: A homework ban would give students who observe religious holidays equal access to those holidays; this is another reason to adopt the ban. Equal access to religious observance matters because it is part of fair treatment at school.

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: A short holiday exemption could replace a complete homework ban. It would preserve time for essential coursework, which is why I prefer the exemption.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: In other words, your exemption proposal would still permit assignments during the holiday. Permitting assignments would still pressure students to choose schoolwork over religious observance, and that is why I support a full ban.

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: Major religious holidays fall on different dates in different communities. Because of that, a single national homework ban would be difficult to schedule.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: Schools can identify major religious holidays through published calendars, which makes a ban practical. In other words, published calendars allow schools to identify the holidays covered by the ban.

utterances.speaker: Bruno

spec.topic: Should ranked-choice voting replace plurality voting in legislative elections?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Ranked-choice voting should replace plurality voting in legislative elections.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The central reason is that plurality voting can elect a legislator without majority support.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That happens because splitting votes among several candidates can allow a candidate opposed by most voters to win under plurality voting.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Under ranked-choice voting, a voter's ballot transfers to a later preference when the voter's preferred candidate is eliminated.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: This gives voters a way to support a preferred candidate without wasting their vote if that candidate is eliminated.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: As a result, ranked-choice voting can produce a winner with support from voters whose first choices were eliminated.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, a winner with support from transferred ballots has a broader mandate than a winner elected only through a plurality of first-choice votes.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Critics are right that replacing plurality voting could make elections confusing for voters, but that objection does not outweigh the democratic benefit.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The reason for the concern is that voters may need to understand several preferences and the elimination process in a ranked-choice election.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, ranked-choice voting transfers ballots according to voters' later preferences after weaker candidates are eliminated.

spec.topic: Should emergency departments charge patients who attend for non-urgent conditions?

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether emergency departments should charge patients who come in with non-urgent conditions. Amir, you start.

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: I say yes, they should charge, because non-urgent patients make up about a third of attendances and they lengthen waits for everyone.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Ayesha, your response?

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: A charge would deter poor patients from coming in even when their condition is serious.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: So you are saying a charge would turn away people who truly need care.

utterances.speaker: Jin
utterances.text: I would say no charge, since many people cannot get a same-day GP appointment. So the emergency department is all they have.

utterances.speaker: Anders
utterances.text: I have worked as a triage nurse for twelve years. Let me tell you what I see.

utterances.speaker: Anders
utterances.text: Patients cannot reliably judge whether their condition is urgent, which is why a charge would be unfair to those who misjudge their symptoms.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Amir, do you have an answer to that?

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: Charging would raise little money, but this is no surprise: collection systems in hospitals are expensive to run.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Put another way, a charge would send people away from care they need.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: We will take a vote after the break.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Your council is debating whether to stock every public toilet with free period products. Where do you stand?

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: Councils should provide free menstrual products in all public toilets, because so many people are caught out away from home without what they need.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What would it cost?

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: It would cost less than one percent of the toilet maintenance budget, which is another reason to do it. I should say I chaired the equalities committee for three years.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer

utterances.speaker: Jelena
