utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: Yes. And there is a further reason: teenage girls often miss school when they cannot afford these products.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer

utterances.speaker: Jelena

utterances.speaker: Interviewer

utterances.speaker: Jelena

utterances.speaker: Jelena

spec.topic: Should governments introduce a tax on vacant homes in areas with housing shortages?

utterances.text: Governments should tax vacant homes where housing is short, since thousands of homes in this city sit empty while families wait on housing lists.

utterances.speaker: Dalia
utterances.text: A tax would give owners a reason to rent out or sell, and that is how it would increase the supply of homes people can live in.

utterances.speaker: Elif

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: My aunt waited two years for a probate decision on her late husband's house, for instance.

utterances.speaker: Dalia

utterances.speaker: Elif

utterances.speaker: Dalia
utterances.text: Exactly, and in other words, owners respond to the incentive: Vancouver saw empty homes fall after its vacancy tax.

utterances.speaker: Dalia
utterances.text: Anyway, I am off to a housing conference next month, so I will bring you the latest figures.

utterances.speaker: Arjun

utterances.speaker: Sunita
utterances.text: That is why they end up refusing to help at home when they do not need money, which is a reason to prefer the flat allowance.

utterances.speaker: Sipho

utterances.speaker: Cillian

utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether an independent commission, rather than legislators, should draw electoral boundaries. Jasper, start us off.

utterances.text: An independent commission should draw the boundaries, because when legislators draw their own districts they get to choose their voters.

utterances.speaker: Camille
utterances.text: But a commission answers to no voters, since its members are never elected.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Valentina, you have studied the commission states.

utterances.speaker: Valentina
utterances.text: Commissions produce more competitive elections, since the share of uncompetitive districts fell by a third in states that adopted them. That is another reason to back Jasper's proposal.

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: Legislators should keep drawing the lines, because voters can throw them out after a bad map.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Camille, so you are saying commissions have no democratic legitimacy?

utterances.speaker: Camille

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: Put another way, Isaac, you want the district lines kept in elected hands.

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: Competitiveness is not the right goal for a map, since a competitive map can still split a city.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So you are saying fair representation of communities matters more than competition.

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: The state legislature redrew our map in a single weekend behind closed doors, which shows how legislators choose their voters.

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: In other words, voters should be able to remove whoever draws the maps: that is what accountability means.

utterances.speaker: Valentina
utterances.text: The next census is due in three years.

spec.format: opinion essay by a single author
spec.topic: Should restaurants automatically add service charges to every bill?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Restaurants should not automatically add service charges to every bill, because a mandatory charge removes the diner's power to reward good service and penalise poor service.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Without that power, servers have less incentive to try hard. And servers who try less hard give diners a worse experience.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I admit that many diners find tipping stressful and confusing.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Automatic charges would spare diners the awkward arithmetic and social pressure of tipping.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: But awkward arithmetic is a small price to pay for keeping control over what one pays.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I once ate at a seaside cafe where the bill carried a charge of twelve percent.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, diners should be free to decide for themselves what a meal was worth.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: There is a second problem: restaurants that add automatic charges keep their menu prices artificially low.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Low menu prices mislead diners about what a meal will actually cost, which is why the practice is a bad one.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, restaurants that add automatic charges mislead diners about the true cost of a meal.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Some restaurants pool the charge and share it among kitchen staff as well as servers.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Pooling the charge is fairer to kitchen staff than leaving them with no share of tips.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: But a voluntary tip can still be pooled in the same way.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: My favourite waiter has worked at the same restaurant for twenty years.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: So, to sum up, an optional, clearly suggested tip is the better compromise.

utterances.text: Tonight's question is whether businesses should give every employee a personal annual training budget. Hiroshi, make the case for the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Hiroshi
utterances.text: Many employees cannot obtain training tailored to their roles. That gap is why I support a personal annual budget for every employee.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: Because many employees cannot obtain role-specific training, every employee should receive a personal annual training budget. Since the same access problem affects workers unevenly, those budgets would also make development opportunities more equitable.

utterances.speaker: Adrian
utterances.text: In other words, many employees lack access to training specific to their roles.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Put another way, employees frequently miss out on learning opportunities designed for their jobs.

utterances.speaker: Adrian
utterances.text: Personal budgets let employees choose courses that are relevant to their work.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: Because workers can choose relevant courses, personal annual budgets would improve the relevance of workplace learning. They would also give employees more ownership of their development for that same reason.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: So you are saying that personal budgets allow workers to select learning that fits their jobs.

utterances.speaker: Hiroshi
utterances.text: Yes, in other words, a personal training budget gives each employee control over course selection.

utterances.speaker: Adrian
utterances.text: Most employees at my company prefer training sessions held in the morning. That scheduling preference is separate from the budget question.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: Since many employees cannot obtain training tailored to their roles, businesses can address those training gaps more directly through personal budgets.

utterances.speaker: Hiroshi

utterances.speaker: Giulia

utterances.speaker: Adrian

utterances.text: For context, I completed a cybersecurity course last spring. Deirdre, what would the closing view be?

utterances.speaker: Josefa

utterances.speaker: Xavier

utterances.speaker: Host

utterances.speaker: Fatima

utterances.text: Pregnant patients often cannot schedule antenatal appointments outside their working hours, and antenatal appointments can identify complications before they become emergencies.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: That matters because unpaid time off for antenatal appointments can impose a financial penalty on pregnant patients.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Some employers would find universal paid time off difficult to administer. Even so, those practical concerns should not outweigh the case for employers offering pregnant patients paid time off for every antenatal appointment.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: I keep my appointment reminders in a paper diary.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: I would also include reasonable travel time, not just the consultation, in any paid entitlement.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: That wider allowance is justified because antenatal appointments can involve unpredictable waiting times. It is also necessary since pregnant patients may have to travel a considerable distance to reach an antenatal clinic.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: So you are proposing paid time for the whole unavoidable journey and appointment, not merely the consultation.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Yes, and paid time off should be available for every scheduled antenatal appointment rather than only for scans or specialist visits.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: In other words, Magnus means that every scheduled antenatal visit should qualify for paid time off. Put another way, Magnus is not limiting the entitlement to appointments that a manager considers medically important.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: I think the entitlement to paid antenatal leave should be protected by law.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: A statutory entitlement could create an administrative burden for small employers, but that burden is not a reason to reject legal protection. A clear legal rule would give employers and pregnant patients consistent expectations.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Employers should also allow pregnant patients some flexibility in choosing appointment times.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: That is practical because flexible scheduling can reduce disruption to colleagues and services.

utterances.speaker: Fiona

spec.topic: Should students be permitted to retake failed exams without their original grades counting?

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: The agenda item is whether students should be allowed to retake failed exams without their original grades counting. Karima, would you begin?

utterances.speaker: Karima
utterances.text: A failed first attempt can depress a student's academic record even after the student later masters the material. That is why a retake without the original grade counting would measure the student's current competence more fairly.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: Before we decide, note that the registrar closes the examination-entry system at five o'clock on Fridays.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: For that reason, I support allowing the retake without the original grade counting. A shared retake rule would give all departments comparable records, which is another reason to adopt the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Karima
utterances.text: A second attempt can show whether a student has learned from feedback on the failed exam. Because of that, the retake process should require students to review the feedback before taking the exam again.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: An original failing grade can help advisers identify students who need academic support. Therefore, advisers should still be able to see that grade even if it does not count toward the final mark.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: Keeping the original grade visible would help employers interpret a student's transcript. It follows that the original grade should remain visible on the transcript even when it does not count toward the final mark.

utterances.speaker: Karima
utterances.text: A common rubric for recording retakes would make transcripts easier to interpret. That is another reason to retain the original grade as a visible but non-counting entry.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: So you are saying that a common rubric would standardize how retakes appear in student records?

utterances.speaker: Karima
utterances.text: Exactly. In other words, a retake without the original grade would measure present competence rather than past failure.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: I have a concern, however: removing the original grade entirely could make it harder to detect repeated academic difficulties. That objection means I cannot support deleting the grade from every record.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: As a separate administrative note, the student union has scheduled its next general meeting for Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: But the claim that the original grade would help employers is not persuasive because employers rarely receive detailed university transcripts. I would not use that point to justify keeping the grade visible.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: Put another way, the retake process would require students to review feedback before making another attempt.

utterances.speaker: Karima
utterances.text: In other words, advisers would retain access to the original failing grade without using it in the final mark.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: To sum up, the transcript would show the original grade without allowing that grade to affect the final mark. We will draft a policy reflecting that distinction.

utterances.text: Companies should require a two-year stay after paying exam fees, since otherwise they end up funding training for their competitors.

utterances.speaker: Daniela

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Lars, you have a view on this.

utterances.speaker: Bilal

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So you are saying the company is already repaid through better work.

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: A pro-rata clause is the fair middle ground. Besides, small firms simply cannot absorb the departure of a newly qualified employee.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: Pro-rata is better, I will grant, because it lets people leave without crippling debt.

utterances.speaker: Bilal

utterances.speaker: Daniela

utterances.speaker: Bilal

spec.topic: Should creators be required to watermark realistic synthetic videos?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Creators should be required to watermark realistic synthetic videos, because a convincing fake can spread to millions of viewers before anyone checks it.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Another reason is that viewers cannot reliably tell synthetic footage from the real thing by eye. In other words, without a visible mark, ordinary viewers cannot judge whether a realistic video is synthetic.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: But watermarks can be cropped out or removed with editing tools.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That objection ignores that invisible watermarks embedded in the file data survive cropping and re-encoding in most tests, which is why removal is harder than it sounds.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A watermark rule would also punish honest creators while malicious actors simply ignore it.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Honest creators already label their work voluntarily, so the rule would mainly give platforms a clear standard for removing unlabelled fakes. Put another way, a labelling rule gives platforms a clear standard for removing unlabelled fakes.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I should say that I edit a small gardening channel.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put simply, requiring watermarks protects public trust in video evidence.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That matters because courts and newsrooms have lately begun to ask for proof of origin for submitted footage.

spec.topic: Should hospitals replace paper consent forms with recorded video explanations?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Hospitals should replace paper consent forms with recorded video explanations because recorded videos can show a procedure's steps and risks in a consistent format.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Patients with limited literacy often struggle with dense medical prose. This is why recorded video explanations can improve the understanding of patients with limited literacy.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The consent office at Northbridge Hospital opens at 7 a.m.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Paper consent forms are the clearest permanent record for patients. But a paper record alone cannot convey tone, demonstrations, or pronunciation, so retaining paper as the primary explanation is inadequate; that limitation is a reason to replace it.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Patients can pause and replay recorded consent videos. Since patients can control the pace, hospitals can offer the same recorded explanation before a clinician answers patients' questions, which is another reason to replace paper forms.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, hospitals ought to exchange paper consent forms for recorded video explanations.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Some patients prefer receiving appointment reminders by text message.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A pilot at three hospitals found that patients who watched consent videos asked more accurate follow-up questions. That finding is another reason hospitals should make the replacement.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, recorded consent explanations let hospitals give patients a repeatable explanation before the question-and-answer stage.

utterances.text: Low-income defendants generally cannot afford private eviction lawyers. That is the reason I support free legal representation in every civil eviction case.

utterances.speaker: Femi
utterances.text: Eviction proceedings can determine whether a family keeps its home, which is why low-income defendants need guaranteed representation.

utterances.speaker: Jasper

utterances.speaker: Femi

utterances.speaker: Femi

spec.topic: Should schools make swimming proficiency a requirement for joining competitive sports teams?

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Should schools make swimming proficiency a requirement for joining competitive sports teams?

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: Yes, because students can encounter deep water during some competitive sports events. Basic swimming proficiency would reduce danger in those situations.

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: The main fairness concern is that some students lack safe access to a swimming pool.

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: For that reason, schools should provide free swimming practice before enforcing a proficiency requirement.

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: In other words, some students do not have safe access to a swimming pool. That is why schools should allow students a preparation period before the swimming test and make passing it a condition of joining a team only after that preparation.

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: The general rule should be that schools require basic swimming proficiency for competitive sports teams. A student who initially fails the test should not be permanently barred from a team.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Would the requirement apply to every team, even teams that never compete near water?

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: Yes; the swimming proficiency requirement should apply to every competitive sports team.

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: However, a universal swimming requirement could exclude talented athletes who lack safe access to a pool. That objection applies both to making the test an immediate condition of joining and to applying the requirement to every team.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So, put another way, passing the swimming test would be a condition of joining a team after students had time to prepare?

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: I have coached junior athletes for six years.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Some schools already record students' emergency contacts digitally.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Should schools make swimming proficiency a requirement for joining competitive sports teams?

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: Competitive sports can leave students exhausted and vulnerable during emergencies. For that reason, schools should require swimming proficiency before students join competitive sports teams.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What practical policy would follow from that concern?

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: Because exhausted athletes may struggle to protect themselves, schools should identify applicants who cannot swim before admitting them to competitive sports teams.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Would the rule involve teaching any particular skills?

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: Yes. Since competitive sports can leave students vulnerable in an emergency, competitive sports teams should teach members how to signal for help in water.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What else should schools provide?

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: The same emergency risk is why schools should keep rescue equipment near pools used by competitive teams. Students who cannot swim should also receive swimming lessons before joining competitive sports teams.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Should proficiency be checked only once?

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: No. Because exhausted students may not retain safety skills, schools should test team members' swimming proficiency every year.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Does the same reasoning affect general team preparation?

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: It does, because vulnerable athletes need a clear response plan; competitive sports teams should practise emergency evacuations.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Would you apply the requirement to every team, including teams that never use a pool?

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: Swimming proficiency should be required even for students joining indoor competitive teams. However, the general risk of exhaustion does not justify making swimming proficiency a condition for every competitive team.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What is your more limited alternative?

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: Schools should identify applicants who cannot swim before admitting them to competitive sports teams. In other words, my position is that schools should identify non-swimmers before admitting them to competitive sports teams.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Before we finish, how did you learn to swim?

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: I learned to swim at the age of seven.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: And how many teams does your school have?

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: My school has six competitive sports teams.

spec.topic: Should national sports federations impose salary caps on professional leagues?

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight: should national sports federations impose salary caps on professional leagues? Rafael, you start.

utterances.speaker: Rafael
utterances.text: Yes, they should, because without caps the richest clubs buy the best players every year.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Ivana, is that a problem?

utterances.speaker: Ivana
utterances.text: A cap makes sense since uncapped competitions become predictable with the same few winners. That matters because fans lose interest when the outcome is predictable.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Bernard, your view?

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: A cap would reduce the gap between rich and poor clubs, which is why I support it.

utterances.speaker: Rafael
utterances.text: But caps push the best players to leagues abroad that pay more, because those players leave and weaken our competition. I have watched this league for thirty years.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Ivana?

utterances.speaker: Ivana
utterances.text: In other words, capped leagues lose their stars, so the quality of play falls.

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: The American leagues use caps and have kept their best players at home, which shows caps can work.

utterances.speaker: Rafael
utterances.text: But those leagues are closed with no relegation, so they are a poor comparison. Put another way, caps work in America because the closed structure protects owners' investments.

utterances.speaker: Ivana
utterances.text: Caps would simply transfer money from players to owners, because owners would keep the savings as profit rather than cut prices.

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: So you are saying the caps would not benefit supporters, since prices would stay the same.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: A quick note: the season starts in August.

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: Still, a cap gives every club a fair chance at the title, so I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: Rafael
utterances.text: In other words, a cap does not make anything cheaper for fans but makes the league fairer.

utterances.speaker: Ivana
utterances.text: A fairer league is worth more to fans than lower prices, so I accept the cap.

utterances.speaker: Host

utterances.text: The American football league has had a cap for decades and its champions change regularly, which shows that caps work in practice to produce balance.

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: I should say I follow the sport mainly on the radio.

utterances.speaker: Ivana

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: Put another way, players keep a fixed share of league revenue under a cap.

utterances.speaker: Ivana
utterances.text: Fans pay for tickets mostly to see star players, which is why losing them abroad would hurt.

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: Ticket sales have risen in capped leagues over the last decade, which backs up my point that caps work.

utterances.speaker: Host

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: Federations are better placed than clubs to enforce a cap fairly, since clubs cannot be trusted to police their own spending.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: I think restorative-justice conferences should replace prosecution for selected juvenile offences. I should say I'm only a volunteer facilitator, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: But dropping prosecution would take away the deterrent for other teenagers.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: That ignores that teenagers rarely weigh penalties before acting, since their impulse control is still developing.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: So you are saying deterrence simply does not work on teenagers.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: Exactly, and conferences cut reoffending, because a local pilot recorded 25 percent reoffending against 40 percent after court.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: But victims may be pressured into forgiving, since some victims in other schemes say they felt obliged to accept an apology.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: Victims choose whether to attend; in other words, nobody is forced to meet the offender.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: So what you mean is the choice sits with the victim.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: Yes. Offenders must admit guilt first, so no innocent juvenile would be pushed through, which is another reason to replace prosecution.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: Repeat offenders need prosecution, since conferences cannot compel any supervision.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: Put another way, repeat offenders would stay with the courts, and I accept that.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: By the way, my nephew went through a school mediation last year.

spec.topic: Should clinical trials be required to include equal numbers of all major demographic groups?

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Our question is whether clinical trials should be required to include equal numbers of all major demographic groups. Nkechi, you support that proposal.

utterances.speaker: Nkechi
utterances.text: Clinical trials should be required to include equal numbers of all major demographic groups. I support that policy because demographic representation affects whether treatment safety is properly assessed.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: But equal demographic quotas can make trial samples less representative of patients in actual practice. I have reviewed clinical-trial protocols for several years.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: The reason I still favor the requirement is that, without equal representation, a treatment can appear safe for one group while harming another. I served on a hospital research committee last spring.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: To put Nkechi's position another way, clinical trials should have equal enrollment from all major demographic groups.

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: Equal enrollment makes comparisons between demographic subgroups more reliable, which is why the requirement is justified. Requiring equal enrollment also forces researchers to test whether results hold across demographic groups, and that is another reason for the requirement.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: So you are saying that the policy is a requirement for equal enrollment across all major demographic groups.

utterances.speaker: Nkechi
utterances.text: Exactly; the proposal requires clinical trials to enroll equal numbers from every major demographic group.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: In other words, the policy would require equal demographic representation in clinical trials. Equal enrollment would also make important differences in treatment response harder to overlook, which is another reason to adopt the requirement.

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: The requirement is also justified because equal demographic enrollment would improve public confidence in clinical-trial evidence. A final reason is that equal enrollment would reduce the risk that medical guidelines are based mainly on evidence from one population.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, Milos, in other words team staff would have no say in whether a replacement is allowed?

utterances.speaker: Hollis

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: Replacements should come in even after the match has started, because concussion symptoms can appear hours after a blow.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Gareth, what kind of player should come on?

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: Put another way, the replacement should be like-for-like, not a specialist.

utterances.speaker: Host

utterances.text: Renata, you have studied the medical evidence, so I will begin with the basic concern.

utterances.text: Marathon runners face a substantial risk of dehydration. Personal hydration support reduces a marathon runner's dehydration risk because of that medical reality.

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: Reducing dehydration risk is a reason to permit personal hydration support, which is why I oppose a ban.

utterances.speaker: Renata

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: Banning personal hydration support would make the race fairer for all competitors.

utterances.speaker: Babajide
utterances.text: I am not persuaded. Runners already differ in the shoes they wear, and that difference is accepted.

utterances.speaker: Babajide
utterances.text: Marathon organisers should permit personal hydration support because reducing dehydration risk is more important than eliminating every difference between runners.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: So you are saying that personal hydration support can create unequal access to water, even though you still think it should be allowed?

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: I would put my own position differently: the marathon should not ban personal hydration support.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: A ban could leave runners without water when official stations are too far away. That is why I do not accept the claim that fairness alone settles the issue.

utterances.speaker: Babajide
utterances.text: Official hydration stations can be placed at regular intervals along the course. Because of that arrangement, regularly spaced official stations can give every runner equal access to water.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: In other words, organisers can make hydration equally available through official stations.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: Official hydration stations may fail to meet runners' needs in extreme heat. In other words, official stations alone may fail to meet runners' needs in extreme heat.

utterances.speaker: Dimitri
utterances.text: Does the medical argument really outweigh the fairness argument?

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: Yes. The marathon should not ban personal hydration support because official stations may be too far apart.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: The course passes through historic city centres in several host cities, which complicates the placement of extra stations.

utterances.speaker: Dimitri
utterances.text: The closing question is whether the organisers should adopt the safer policy. My summary is that the marathon should not ban personal hydration support.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: Our question is whether teachers should be allowed to grade class participation as part of final marks. Aurelio, please begin.

utterances.speaker: Aurelio
utterances.text: Teachers should be allowed to include class participation in final marks. Class participation can show whether students have prepared and engaged with lessons, which is why I support the policy.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: Some students contribute more effectively in writing than in spoken classroom discussion. More importantly, participation grades can disadvantage students who are quiet or anxious; that is why I oppose including them in final marks.

utterances.speaker: Arjun
utterances.text: A clear participation rubric can specify preparation, listening, and constructive contribution. Because those criteria can be stated in advance, a clear participation rubric makes grading less arbitrary.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: Teachers can publish the participation rubric before the course begins. That makes the grading criteria transparent.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: So you are saying that publishing the rubric in advance makes the grading criteria transparent?

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: Exactly. Transparent criteria let teachers assess participation consistently across the term, and consistent assessment across the term gives teachers evidence of sustained engagement.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: For the record, the debate is taking place during the final week of the school year.

utterances.speaker: Aurelio
utterances.text: Regular participation grades can reward students who prepare consistently, because regular participation gives teachers evidence from more than one assignment.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: Orla, is that different from saying that participation rewards consistent preparation over time?

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: No, that is exactly the point: participation grades can reward consistent preparation over time. They should not, however, determine most of a student's final mark.

utterances.speaker: Arjun
utterances.text: I agree that participation should count for only a small share of a student's final mark. A limited weighting protects the broader assessment from overreliance on classroom speaking.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: In other words, participation grading should not determine most of a student's final mark?

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: Yes. Some students need alternative ways to demonstrate engagement because speaking publicly can be difficult for them; schools should therefore offer alternative evidence of engagement to students who cannot demonstrate it through frequent speaking.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: In other words, a fair participation grade concerns the quality of preparation and engagement, not the number of times a student speaks. Defining participation by quality rather than speaking frequency would reduce the advantage held by naturally talkative students.

utterances.speaker: Aurelio

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: Because the criteria must be clear, schools should publish them before allowing participation to affect final marks. That publication would make participation marks easier for students to understand and challenge.

spec.topic: Should governments build desalination plants despite their high energy use and marine impacts?

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight: should governments build desalination plants despite the energy use and marine impacts? Wilhelmina, you start.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: Yes, they should, because coastal cities cannot rely on rainfall alone as droughts grow longer and more frequent.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Gareth, what is wrong with that?

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: Desalination gives a supply that does not depend on rainfall, in other words a source that works through a drought.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Gareth?

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: These plants burn enormous amounts of electricity, which is why they are too energy-hungry to be a responsible choice.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tariq?

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: But solar and wind farms built alongside them can power the plants, so the energy cost is largely removable.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Gareth, a personal note?

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: I have lived in a drought-hit town for ten years.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: And the marine side?

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: Brine discharge raises salinity near outfalls and harms seabed life.

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: That marine damage is a serious cost, since the brine harms the seabed.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: Diffusers spreading brine over a wide area dilute it quickly, which is a reason to doubt how serious the damage is.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Gareth, alternatives?

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: Fixing leaking pipes would save more water than a new plant, because marine damage is a serious cost.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Let me sum up Gareth: so you are saying desalination is too energy-hungry to be a responsible choice, given huge electricity use.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: And Wilhelmina, so you are saying dry cities need a supply independent of rainfall.

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: The pipe-fixing programme in the region began last year.

utterances.speaker: Dimitri
utterances.text: Our question is whether marathon organisers should ban personal hydration support. Leopold, you support a ban.

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: Personal hydration teams can give some runners more reliable access to fluids than other runners receive. Because that advantage undermines equal conditions, organisers should ban runners from using personal hydration support.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: Some runners need fluids delivered at particular times because of medical conditions. Banning personal hydration support could therefore endanger runners with specific medical needs.

utterances.speaker: Babajide
utterances.text: The marathon course passes the city's old athletics stadium. A ban would make it simpler for officials to enforce one hydration rule.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: I have volunteered at six marathons, and enforcement is rarely simple.

utterances.speaker: Dimitri
utterances.text: Official hydration stations can supply runners evenly along the course, so evenly placed official stations would reduce the competitive advantage of personal support teams.

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: A ban would allow officials to check one hydration system instead of several private arrangements. Checking one hydration system would reduce disputes about unauthorised assistance.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: However, medical needs make a completely uniform hydration rule unsafe; that convenience does not settle the safety issue.

utterances.speaker: Babajide
utterances.text: So you are saying that some runners require fluids at medically determined times.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Personal hydration teams give better-supported runners an advantage over runners who rely only on official stations. For that reason, banning personal hydration support would make the competition fairer.

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: In other words, medical requirements make a single hydration rule potentially unsafe. That concern should be addressed through narrowly defined exemptions rather than unrestricted personal support.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: But a ban would still disadvantage runners whose medical needs cannot be covered by narrow exemptions.

spec.topic: Should teachers be allowed to grade class participation as part of final marks?

utterances.speaker: Aurelio
utterances.text: Our question tonight is whether teachers should be allowed to count class participation toward final marks. Orla, you support the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: Yes. Participation marks can recognize work that is invisible in written assignments, and teachers should be allowed to include class participation in final marks.

utterances.speaker: Arjun
utterances.text: I am cautious about that. Participation grades can disadvantage quiet students, and they can reward confidence rather than understanding.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: The answer is a published rubric. Such a rubric can make participation grading more consistent, and published criteria can tell students exactly what participation means.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: To put Orla's point another way, class participation can reveal preparation that written tests miss. That benefit matters even when a student does not speak constantly.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: I would also require a clear participation rubric, because a clear rubric makes grading more consistent. Allowing private reflections would broaden the evidence used for participation marks.

utterances.speaker: Arjun
utterances.text: A private reflection can record contributions from quieter students. Teachers can therefore assess preparation without rewarding students merely for speaking often.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: Private reflections can record contributions from quieter students; in addition, schools can audit grades that are based on a participation rubric.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: For context, Orla has taught history for twelve years.

utterances.speaker: Aurelio
utterances.text: The studio audience contains several trainee teachers. Arjun, give us your final objection.

utterances.speaker: Arjun
utterances.text: Participation grades can favor outspoken students over reflective students. That is why I object to allowing participation in final marks, although the problem could be reduced with a broader assessment.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: A clear participation rubric makes grading more consistent. Because of that safeguard, teachers should be allowed to use participation marks, and published criteria can tell students exactly what participation means.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: Tonight's question is whether teachers should be allowed to count class participation toward final marks. Aurelio, you support the idea.

utterances.speaker: Aurelio
utterances.text: Participation can reveal preparation and collaborative understanding that written tests may miss. For that reason, teachers should be allowed to include class participation in students' final marks.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: A participation grade can reward students who help classmates understand difficult material. That is why teachers should be allowed to grade class participation when it rewards that kind of help.

utterances.speaker: Arjun
utterances.text: Some students demonstrate their understanding more clearly in discussion than in timed examinations. In other words, participation marks can recognize understanding that timed examinations fail to capture.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: A clearly published participation rubric can make classroom contributions assessable. Consequently, teachers should be allowed to use a published rubric when awarding participation marks.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: A further benefit is that participation grades can encourage students to listen carefully to one another. That can improve the quality of classroom discussion.

utterances.speaker: Aurelio
utterances.text: Quiet students may be disadvantaged when speaking frequently is treated as the main sign of participation. Put another way, a participation grade can unfairly favor frequent speakers over quiet students.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: A fair system should count listening, written contributions and small-group work as participation. So a fair participation system should assess several kinds of classroom contribution.

utterances.speaker: Arjun
utterances.text: Students' access to confidence, free time and language fluency differs. Therefore, participation marks can reflect unequal advantages in confidence, free time and language fluency.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: Those unequal advantages make participation grades less reliable than teachers often assume. I am not rejecting the proposal, but this is a serious objection to treating participation as a simple measure.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: The transparent alternative is to allow participation grades only under a transparent and inclusive system, because Aurelio's point about measuring collaborative understanding still matters and Orla's point about helping classmates supports that safeguard.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: So Giulia is saying that participation may count, but only when the assessment includes more than frequent speaking.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: Exactly. The panel is debating assessment policy rather than attendance requirements.

utterances.speaker: Arjun
utterances.text: The final marks are issued at the end of the academic year.

utterances.speaker: Arjun

But that same problem is precisely why teachers should not be given a general permission to grade participation.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: Participation is not just talking: it includes listening, asking questions, and contributing to group work. In other words, participation is more than the frequency with which a student speaks, and that broader measure supports allowing teachers to grade it.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: A clear participation rubric makes expectations visible to students. Those visible expectations can help quieter students understand how to contribute, which is another reason to permit participation marks.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: Final marks should reflect demonstrated learning. Participation can provide evidence of that demonstrated learning, so it belongs among the forms of evidence a teacher may consider.

utterances.speaker: Arjun
utterances.text: The difficulty is that participation is shaped partly by disability, language, and anxiety. Because of those circumstances, grading participation can penalize students for reasons unrelated to mastery, and it can also pressure them to perform agreement instead of thinking critically.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: Teachers can accept alternative forms of participation, such as written questions or prepared group roles. That is why participation grading can be equitable when students are offered alternative forms of participation.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: Teachers already judge oral presentations and collaborative work. Since participation grading draws on those familiar classroom judgments, it would not require an entirely unfamiliar kind of judgment.

utterances.speaker: Arjun
utterances.text: My objection remains that participation marks can pressure students to perform agreement instead of thinking critically. Put another way, alternative forms of participation can accommodate different ways for students to contribute, but they do not automatically remove the pressure created by a graded classroom conversation.

utterances.speaker: Aurelio
utterances.text: The disagreement is clear: one side sees participation as useful evidence, while the other stresses fairness and student autonomy. We will return to the question after the break.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: For context, I have taught history for eleven years.

spec.topic: Should political parties face strict limits on total campaign spending?

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: Parties should face strict limits on total campaign spending, since wealthy parties can drown out their rivals with advertising. Elections ought to be decided by ideas rather than by budgets, which is another reason.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: But limits restrict the ability of parties to communicate with voters.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: Do you mean that limits would silence smaller parties as much as larger ones?

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo

spec.topic: Should public hospitals offer free genetic testing for patients with a strong family history of inherited disease?

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight: should public hospitals offer free genetic testing to patients with a strong family history of inherited disease? Thandiwe, you start.

utterances.speaker: Thandiwe
utterances.text: They should, because early detection lets doctors start preventive treatment before symptoms appear. And preventive treatment is far cheaper than treating advanced disease.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: I have watched this up close; my aunt was diagnosed at forty.

utterances.speaker: Thandiwe
utterances.text: Which shows that free testing would save the health service money in the long run, and that is the reason hospitals should offer it.

utterances.speaker: Host

utterances.text: But many patients who test positive would suffer lasting anxiety, since many inherited conditions have no available treatment.

utterances.speaker: Host

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: Patients should be allowed to decline after counselling, because counselling before and after testing reduces the distress of those who get bad news.

utterances.speaker: Thandiwe
utterances.text: Put another way, free testing means nobody is deprived of care because of their income.

utterances.speaker: Host

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: A swimming requirement could exclude students who have had fewer opportunities to learn swimming. Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: Schools should provide a basic swimming lesson before team selection, because the same emergency risk makes preparation necessary.

utterances.speaker: Keiko

utterances.speaker: Interviewer

utterances.speaker: Interviewer

utterances.text: Our question is whether marathon organisers should ban runners from using personal hydration support. Dimitri, make the case for a ban.

utterances.speaker: Dimitri
utterances.text: Personal hydration support gives some runners access to water beyond the official aid stations. Because that creates unequal access on the course, marathon organisers should ban personal hydration support.

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: I disagree with that conclusion: a ban on personal hydration support would endanger runners in hot weather.

utterances.speaker: Babajide
utterances.text: Official aid stations can be spaced six kilometres apart. Since those gaps can leave runners without water for a long period, the spacing is a serious safety concern.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: In other words, official aid stations may leave runners waiting a long time for their next drink. I volunteer at a marathon each autumn.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: Leopold, are safety concerns enough to reject a complete ban?

utterances.speaker: Dimitri
utterances.text: Long gaps between aid stations make personal hydration support necessary for some runners. For that reason, marathon organisers should allow personal hydration support under clear rules.

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: So you are saying that personal hydration support should be allowed under clear rules.

utterances.speaker: Babajide
utterances.text: Since organisers could register each support vehicle and restrict where it stops, a permit system for personal hydration support would be easy for organisers to enforce. That would improve compliance with hydration rules.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: On the contrary, personal hydration support does not necessarily create unequal race conditions; runners still have to complete the same course.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: Dimitri has raised fairness, while Leopold and Elif have raised safety. What practical compromise could address both?

utterances.speaker: Renata

utterances.text: Our question tonight is whether teachers should be allowed to grade class participation as part of final marks. Orla, you support the idea.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: Teachers should be allowed to include class participation in final marks. Class participation gives teachers evidence of students' preparation and engagement, which is why it belongs in the final assessment.

utterances.speaker: Arjun
utterances.text: I disagree: class participation should not count toward final marks. Participation grades can disadvantage students who are shy or have communication difficulties, because speaking frequently is not the same as understanding the material.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: The school library closes at six on Fridays.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: Participation grades can capture preparation and peer help that examinations miss. They are useful because students reveal their understanding by explaining ideas aloud.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: So, in other words, teachers should be allowed to assess classroom engagement as part of final marks.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: A clear participation rubric would make grading more consistent, because a clear rubric would reduce the influence of personal impressions on participation grades.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: So you are saying that a clear rubric would make participation grading more consistent. That is why participation grades can measure observable academic contribution.

utterances.speaker: Arjun
utterances.text: Regular contributions can reveal whether students have prepared for class.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: Put another way, participation grades can measure observable academic contribution because regular contributions can reveal whether students have prepared for class.

utterances.speaker: Damien

utterances.text: Our question tonight is whether teachers should be allowed to grade class participation as part of final marks. Orla, you support the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: Participation is difficult to measure consistently across classrooms. For context, this debate is taking place during the station's evening programme.

utterances.speaker: Arjun
utterances.text: A participation grade can include a student's questions, explanations and contributions to group work. The important issue is whether teachers can judge those contributions fairly.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: Teachers should not be allowed to grade participation as part of final marks. That is because participation grades can penalize students who need more time to formulate their thoughts.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: They can also disadvantage students who are learning in a second language.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: Teachers observe students' classroom contributions more regularly than they observe students' independent study. Because of that regular observation, teachers can gather useful evidence about students' understanding from classroom contributions.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: That evidence matters because participation marks can reward students who explain ideas clearly to their classmates.

utterances.speaker: Aurelio
utterances.text: A well-designed participation rubric can distinguish frequent speaking from constructive contribution. The difficulty is that participation scores can reflect classroom confidence more than academic understanding.

utterances.speaker: Aurelio
utterances.text: Put another way, participation scores can reflect classroom confidence more than academic understanding. That is why teachers should be allowed to include participation in final marks when they use a transparent rubric.

utterances.speaker: Aurelio
utterances.text: A transparent rubric would give students a clear account of how participation affects their marks, which is another reason to permit the practice.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: So you are saying that participation should not mean simply talking the most.

utterances.speaker: Aurelio
utterances.text: Exactly. In other words, a participation grade should be based on several forms of contribution rather than on speaking often. Using several forms of contribution would make participation assessment fairer.

utterances.speaker: Aurelio
utterances.text: It would also recognize listening and collaborative work, because those activities are part of classroom learning.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: The difficulty of measuring participation consistently is the central objection to using it in final marks. Still, a transparent rubric can answer that objection.

utterances.speaker: Arjun
utterances.text: To put the definition plainly, a participation grade can include questions, explanations and contributions to group work. That makes it broader than a tally of how many times a student speaks.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: The panel has therefore distinguished frequent speaking from broader classroom contribution, while acknowledging concerns about consistency.

utterances.speaker: Aurelio

utterances.speaker: Orla

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: Arjun, what is your strongest objection?

utterances.speaker: Arjun
utterances.text: Participation grades can unfairly penalize students who contribute quietly.

utterances.speaker: Arjun

utterances.speaker: Aurelio

utterances.speaker: Aurelio

spec.topic: Should councils ban petrol-powered leaf blowers on public land?

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight: should councils ban petrol-powered leaf blowers on public land? Ifeoma, start us off.

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: Yes, they should, because petrol blowers produce noise above safe limits for residents. They also pump fine particulates and fumes out at ground level, which is exactly where children breathe.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Kieran, you are not convinced.

utterances.speaker: Kieran
utterances.text: Battery blowers are too weak to clear wet leaves from big parks.

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: That is not what we found, since my council trialled battery blowers last autumn and cleared its parks without delays.

utterances.speaker: Kieran
utterances.text: Battery blowers also cost a lot more to buy. Sunita, your council is replacing its depot vehicles next year, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Sunita
utterances.text: It is, yes. Kieran, I gather you grew up next to a municipal park.

utterances.speaker: Kieran
utterances.text: I did. And a ban would be unaffordable for councils, because it would force them to buy new equipment.

utterances.speaker: Sunita
utterances.text: Battery blowers are cheaper to run, since they need no fuel and little servicing.

utterances.speaker: Sunita
utterances.text: So over a few years they cost less overall than petrol ones, and that is a reason to support the ban.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, Kieran, you are saying a ban would be unaffordable for councils.

utterances.speaker: Kieran
utterances.text: Not only that: gardeners could just use rakes and brooms on most paths. In other words, mechanical clearing is a workable alternative.

spec.topic: Should political parties face strict limits on total campaign spending?

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: Parties should face strict limits on total campaign spending, because without limits the ones with wealthy donors simply drown out everyone else.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: Why would a cap be fairer? Parties would still find ways around it.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: Limits also ease the pressure to court large donors, which is another reason to have them.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: But limits restrict the ability of parties to talk to voters at all.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: Capping spending forces parties to compete on ideas rather than on advertising budgets. In other words, a cap makes parties win arguments instead of buying airtime.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: I have volunteered for a party in two elections, so I have seen the work involved.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: What I mean is that a cap is just a cap on how many voters get informed.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: Not so: limits can be set high enough that every party still runs a full campaign.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: Where do you get that from?

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: So you can see that parties would still be able to reach every voter under limits of that kind. I read a report on it last winter.
